newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: In South Korea, politics not money drives strikers.
newsitem.headline: In South Korea, politics not money drives strikers.

text.p: South Korean auto worker Ko Young-min has hardly a care in the world. His brand new car is paid for with a no-interest company loan, and his comfortable apartment is crammed with modern luxuries.
Part of the country's blue-collar elite, the 34 year-old Ko tests engines for a living at Kia Motors.

When overtime payments are added to his salary, he takes home the equivalent of about US$2,400 a month. His wife quit her job after their two children came along, but he's happy enough without the extra money.
Yet Ko is now on strike, joining stoppages that have crippled the country's industry, including his own car plant.

It is not demands for a fatter pay check that have brought Ko to the picket lines, but opposition to a government that he feels is trying to crush the union movement with a new labour law that gives companies the right to fire workers.
"The government is using this evil law to weaken the unions," he said.

Since 1987, when South Koreans won their battle for democracy, workers like Ko have scored impressive victories in another struggle -- to grab their share of the wealth of Asia's booming "Tiger" economy.
Powerful unions have helped secure pay increases averaging 15 percent per year. Ko's take-home salary today is 10 times greater than in 1988.
But pay increases have far outstripped productivity and a jobs-for-life labour system has further eroded South Korea's competitiveness.
The labour law is one way the government is tackling the problem.
Ko's job is now less secure. But job security is not the issue for for Cho Byung-kil, a welder in a factory that makes pedals and windshield wipers for Kia cars.
"I don't have to worry about losing my job because no one wants to work under the conditions of middle- and small-sized companies," said Cho, 35.

Cho earns 40 percent less than Ko -- $1,400 a month, working 60-hour weeks. Only by racking up overtime can he support his family. He is not on strike, but is cheering on the militant unions organising the stoppages.
"We are producing less now because the automobile industry has been halted," Cho said.
Ko confesses to a guilty conscience over a growing income gap between employees of blue-chip firms, such as his own, and union comrades struggling in smaller enterprises.
"I can drive my new car, not because the employers are cutting us a piece of their profits, but because they have squeezed the contractor making the auto parts," Ko said.
"The more I get, the less the workers under the contractors for Kia get," he said apologetically.

While strikes that helped topple what is now called "military dictatorship" in the 1980s were about higher pay and decent work conditions, the latest round of industrial unrest is "Labour strikes go beyond a demand for higher wages," said Yi Chong-kak, a weathered 40-year old woman and veteran of the union movement since the 1970s when she toiled over cotton spools in a textile factory.
"It's a political fight to prevent the annihilation of the labour movement."
